Q: Use "terra::predict" with a "quantregForest" model and get the standard deviation of predictions A:

I use a minimal, self-contained, reproducible example to facilitate answering your questions.

When using terra::predict with a quantregForest object, what=sd works. With a caret train object it is ignored because caret::predict.train does not forward what to quantregForest::predict.quantregForest.

Example data

library(terra)
logo <- rast(system.file("ex/logo.tif", package = "terra"))
set.seed(1)
s <- spatSample(logo, 200, "random", na.rm = TRUE, as.df = TRUE)
s$y <- with(s, 0.5 * red + 0.3 * green + 0.2 * blue + rnorm(nrow(s), 0, 10))

Fit a model and predict

library(quantregForest)
qrf <- quantregForest(x = s[, c("red", "green", "blue")], y = s$y,  ntree = 50)

# Same pattern as the glm se.fit custom fun example in ?terra::predict
predfun <- function(model, data, ...) {
  cbind(
    mean = predict(model, data, what = mean),
    sd   = predict(model, data, what = sd)
  )
}

out <- predict(logo, qrf, fun = predfun, na.rm = TRUE)
plot(out)

# Or the equivalent by passing what= through ... (like se.fit=TRUE in the glm example)
sd_only <- predict(logo, qrf, na.rm=TRUE, what=sd)

If the fitted object is a caret train model, use model$finalModel (a quantregForest) instead (and you figured that out).

To use a categorical variable, you do not need to dummy- or one-hot-encode in this case. You can do

library(terra)
library(quantregForest)

flogo <- rast(system.file("ex/logo.tif", package = "terra"))
flogo$red <- classify(flogo$red, c(-1, 85, 170, 256)) 
# flogo$red is a factor

set.seed(1)
dat <- spatSample(flogo, 300, "random", na.rm = TRUE, as.df = TRUE)
dat$y <- with(dat, 0.4 * as.numeric(red) + 0.3 * green + 0.2 * blue + rnorm(nrow(dat), 0, 8))

qrf_fac <- quantregForest(x = dat[, c("red", "green", "blue")], y = dat$y, ntree = 400)
out_fac <- predict(flogo, qrf_fac, na.rm = TRUE, what = mean)

But you can...

## One-hot with terra::segregate (all 3 classes)
oh <- segregate(flogo$red)
names(oh) <- c("A", "B", "C")
ohlogo <- c(flogo[[2:3]], oh)

set.seed(1)
dat_oh <- spatSample(ohlogo, 300, "random", na.rm = TRUE)
dat_oh$y <- dat$y

qrf_oh <- quantregForest(x=dat_oh[, c("green", "blue", "A", "B", "C")],  y=dat_oh$y, ntree = 400)
out_oh <- predict(ohlogo, qrf_oh, na.rm = TRUE, what = mean)

## Dummy encoding — drop reference class A
set.seed(1)
qrf_dum <- quantregForest(x=dat_oh[, c("green", "blue", "B", "C")], y=dat_oh$y, ntree = 400)
out_dum <- predict(ohlogo, qrf_dum, na.rm = TRUE, what = mean)

pairs(c(out_fac, out_oh, out_dum))

Very similar results --- not the same, they are not the same models. One variable becomes two or three variables. I do not know why you get missing values. I expect it is because of name/level mismatches, or because there are values outside the training factor levels, not from omitting the reference class. Either way, I would not use the dummy encoding in this case.

Q: Why does a Python subprocess hang only when stdout is redirected to PIPE? A:

As indicated by the comments posted to your question, you can hang unless the streams created by your Popen call, i.e. p.stdout and p.stderr, are concurrently being read while they are being written. So, you have two options:

Option 1

You can use Popen.communicate instead of Popen.wait:

import subprocess

p = subprocess.Popen(
    ["dir"],
    shell=True,
    text=True,
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
    stderr=subprocess.PIPE
)

stdout_output, stderr_output = p.communicate()
print(stdout_output, end='')
print(stderr_output, end='')

Option 2

Using Popen.communicate works, but you will not get any of the stdout and stderr output until the subprocess terminates. If you want to process the output as it is being generated, continue to use Popen.wait. But now you must arrange to have those streams read as they are being written to avoid blocking. For this we can use multithreading:

import subprocess
import threading

def process_stream(stream_name, stream):
    for line in iter(stream.readline, ''):
        print(f'{stream_name}: {line}', end='', flush=True)

p = subprocess.Popen(
    ["dir"],
    shell=True,
    text=True,
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
    stderr=subprocess.PIPE
)

threads = [
    threading.Thread(target=process_stream, args=args)
    for args in (('stdout', p.stdout), ('stderr', p.stderr))
]

for t in threads:
    t.start()

p.wait()

for t in threads:
    t.join()

Q: Difference between claud.ai vs platform.claude.com A:

claude.ai is a simple web‑chat interface aimed at occasional users. It requires no API key, has a free tier, and offers only the default Claude model with limited configuration options.

platform.claude.com is the developer portal. It provides API keys, usage‑based billing, the ability to pick different Claude models, access to the workbench for prompt testing, and other management features. It is intended for regular or heavy integration work and expects you to track spend yourself.

In short, use claude.ai for quick, informal chats. Use platform.claude.com when you need programmatic access, billing visibility, or model selection.

Q: MyPy: Can not suppress [no-untyped-call] A:

As comments pointed out, the configuration there applied if you type checked the numpy module, not when type checking calls into numpy.

New versions of mypy give you a way to selectively ignore specific untyped calls, see this configuration option: https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/command_line.html#cmdoption-mypy-untyped-calls-exclude

(Also new versions of numpy have type annotations!)
